findings.scenario: 1) Victim node V dials any node M (e.g. via `peer add-url`, bootstrap_urls, or an invite whose peer_info_url points at M). V's connect() sends `HLO1 || len || msgpack(SignedHello)` on its first bidi stream. 2) M stores the ~200-byte blob. 3) M opens a QUIC connection to target S (S's server does `with_no_client_auth`, so any client is accepted) and writes V's SignedHello verbatim. 4) S's accept() verifies the ed25519 signature (valid, it is V's) and `peer_id == blake3(pk)[:20]`, then `connections.insert(V, attacker_conn)`, overwriting V's genuine entry. 5) dispatch_peer_streams attributes every TXFR/GSP1/DHT1/BSW1 stream from M to V, and S's `open_stream(V)` / FileWant pushes now go to M. The blob never expires because ts_ms is signed but unchecked.
findings.impact_ai_game: PeerId is the only identity on the data plane. A replayed Hello lets an outsider push asset versions as a trusted artist/CI/history node and receive files intended for that node, i.e. silent substitution and exfiltration of unreleased game and AI assets. It also makes any future PeerId-based membership ACL (the main security redesign item) worthless, since the ACL would admit the replayed identity.
findings.current_state: One-way TLS pinning (client verifies server SPKI) plus an application-layer signed Hello with no freshness or channel binding; the operations-readiness doc claims mutual authentication is done.
findings.proposed_redesign: Make the QUIC/TLS layer carry both identities: (1) server `ServerConfig::builder().with_client_cert_verifier(Arc<PeerPinningClientVerifier>)` where the verifier extracts the ed25519 SPKI exactly like PeerPinningVerifier and derives the PeerId; client `with_client_auth_cert(cert, key)` from the same Identity (rcgen self-signed); `connection.peer_identity()` yields the authenticated PeerId on both sides. (2) Reduce HLO1 to a metadata frame {protocol_version, capabilities, membership_credential} that must name the TLS-derived PeerId; reject mismatch. (3) If a non-mTLS fallback is kept (relay path), sign `b"synergos/hello/v2" || tls_exporter("synergos-hello", 32B via export_keying_material) || server_nonce(16B) || ts_ms`, server sends the nonce first, reject |now - ts_ms| > 120 s. (4) Registry policy: a second connection for an already-connected PeerId is closed with an explicit error unless the existing one is dead; or key the map by (PeerId, ConnectionId) with explicit selection. (5) ALPN `synergos/1`.
alternatives: Noise IK handshake inside QUIC datagrams (rejected: duplicates TLS 1.3 and loses quinn's integration)
Keep HLO1 and only enforce a ts_ms window (insufficient: replay inside the window still succeeds and clocks drift)

findings.scenario: A user follows the mesh checklist and runs `synergos peer add-url http://192.0.2.10:7780` (or sets bootstrap_urls). An on-path host on the mesh/LAN, a rogue not-yet-revoked mesh member, or a DNS/ARP spoofer answers the plaintext GET /peer-info with its own `peer_id` and `quic_endpoint`. Because expected_peer is None, the daemon pins the attacker's PeerId (expected_peer_id = advertised) and the TLS pinning 'succeeds' against the attacker. The daemon then registers the attacker as a peer of every open project (bootstrap_urls path) and starts exchanging FileOffer/FileWant/TXFR with it. Only the invite-token path (which carries host_peer_id) is immune.
findings.impact_ai_game: Studio onboarding is exactly this flow (two-node checklist). One spoofed bootstrap turns an outsider into a full peer that receives every gossip offer and can push versions into working trees.
findings.current_state: Invite path pins host_peer_id (good); `peer add-url` and `bootstrap_urls` are TOFU; peer-info is unsigned JSON over http; docs contradict the code comment on binding.
findings.proposed_redesign: Replace /peer-info with a signed node card: `{peer_id, pubkey, endpoints[], protocol_version, synergos_version, issued_at, expires_at, sig}` where sig = Ed25519 over `b"synergos/node-card/v1" || canonical(card)`; the client verifies pubkey->peer_id and signature before any DNS/QUIC work and caches the card until expires_at. Require the expected PeerId on every non-invite bootstrap: `bootstrap = [{ url = "...", peer_id = "<40 hex>" }]` in TOML and `peer add-url --peer <id>` in the CLI (reject without it). Apply the same plaintext policy as control_heartbeat (`http` only to loopback or 192.0.2.10/12, else https). Fix the checklist to bind peer-info to the mesh IP, not 0.0.0.0.
alternatives: https everywhere (hard with IP-literal mesh addresses and no PKI)
DNSSEC/DoH-anchored names (mesh resolver code is dormant today)

findings.scenario: A lead runs `project invite <id>` without --expires and pastes the `syn1.` token into Slack for a vendor. Months later the vendor is off-boarded; the token (in chat history, a ticket, an exported channel) still decodes (expires_at None), the nonce is never checked, the host keeps no record of issued tokens, and the joiner bootstraps to host_peer_id and joins. The issuing host cannot revoke it without rotating its node identity (which is itself unsupported, SEC-CR-09).
findings.impact_ai_game: External vendors are a primary persona (ux-definition 外部受託者). Standing, unexpiring access credentials are the common thread of the studio breaches catalogued in the research (Rockstar, Okta, CircleCI): a leaked invite is a permanent door into a project's asset stream.
findings.current_state: Signed by host identity (payload integrity ok), expiry optional, no server-side state, no join handshake; legacy UUID invites are one-shot but daemon-local only.
findings.proposed_redesign: Invite v2 payload `{project_id, host_peer_id, host_pubkey, peer_info_url, invitee_pubkey?, iat, exp (required; default 24 h, max 7 d), nonce (16 B), uses}` signed with context `synergos/invite/v2`. Host persists an invite ledger (nonce -> uses_remaining, revoked) and the join becomes an authenticated protocol: joiner opens a `JOIN1` stream over its mTLS/HLO1-authenticated connection, presents the token and (if invitee_pubkey set) proves that key; host checks exp, nonce, uses, marks consumed, records `(project_id, joiner_peer_id)` in its membership registry and returns a membership credential. CLI: `project invite --expires` required (reject none), `project invite revoke <nonce>`, `project invite ls`.
alternatives: Biscuit capability tokens issued by Cernere with attenuation and revocation ids (better long term; requires Cernere root key and control-plane revocation feed)
Keep bearer tokens but short default TTL only (does not solve multi-use or revocation)

findings.scenario: Curare's environment (or its Infisical scope, a Curare RCE, a backup of the Curare host) leaks SYNERGOS_RECEIPT_SECRET. The holder computes HMAC(secret, canonical({method:"GET",key:sha256(blobRef),expires:2^62,name:"x"})) for any blobRef listed in Curare's asset_versions and downloads every object through the public transfer endpoint, bypassing the custody admin token entirely; they can also forge a 'durable' receipt for an object that was never stored, defeating the custody evidence Curare relies on to create versions. No key id exists, so rotation is a simultaneous flag day for both services.
findings.impact_ai_game: Custody is the durable anchor for release artifacts; the spec's whole point is that Curare cannot fake durability and custody cannot interpret versions. A shared symmetric secret collapses that boundary and makes the release evidence unverifiable by anyone but the two parties holding the secret.
findings.current_state: HMAC-SHA256 with a single secret; constant-time verify is correct; separate `token` exists but is compared through the same secret; Curare also exposes a push `POST /storage/receipts` that accepts client-relayed receipts verified with the same secret.
findings.proposed_redesign: (1) Receipts: Ed25519 detached signatures by a custody-node signing key; Curare configured with `SYNERGOS_RECEIPT_PUBKEYS={"<kid>":"<base64 pubkey>"}`; receipt carries `kid`, `alg:"Ed25519"`, `iat`, `nonce`. (2) Capabilities: a custody-only key `cap_key` (never shared), or HKDF-SHA256(root, info="synergos-custody/cap/v1") if one root secret must stay; include `kid` in the URL/header. (3) Bearer compare: `subtle::ConstantTimeEq` over SHA-256(provided) vs SHA-256(expected) with no secret involved. (4) Rotation: accept two kids during a grace window; receipts/capabilities name their kid. (5) Remove Curare's push receipt route or make it verify with the public key and node-location check.
alternatives: Macaroons (still shared secret; verifier can mint)
Biscuit tokens for capabilities (public-key, attenuable; larger change but aligns with SEC-CR-03/05)

findings.scenario: An artist requests an acquisition plan (up to 1000 signed GET URLs). The plan JSON sits in browser devtools/history, a Slack paste, a reverse-proxy or CDN access log in front of custody (signature is in the query string), or is read by a malicious browser extension. Anyone replays each URL within 900 s (custody cap) and gets the bytes; custody writes no access record, so the exfiltration is invisible and unattributable. PUT capabilities can likewise be replayed to start parallel partial uploads until expiry.
findings.impact_ai_game: Bulk plan issuance is the normal clone workflow, so a single leak equals a whole-release dump; the GTA6/Insomniac incidents were volume exfiltrations that only download-attribution and anomaly detection would have caught.
findings.current_state: HMAC(method,key,expires,name), 15 min PUT / <=900 s GET, no jti, no caller binding, no logging, signature in URL.
findings.proposed_redesign: (1) Move the capability to `Authorization: Capability <base64url(token)>` for SDK/CLI clients; keep URL form only for browser downloads with TTL <= 120 s. (2) Single-use: add `jti` (16 B) to the signed message; custody keeps a bounded seen-set keyed by expiry and rejects reuse. (3) Sender constraint: Curare puts `sub=<cernere user id>` and the client's device public key into the capability; client signs (method, key, jti, ts) with that key per request (DPoP-style); custody verifies. (4) Structured access log `{capability_id, sub, key, method, remote_addr, bytes, outcome}` shipped to the control plane for per-identity volume baselines. (5) Optional signed byte-range (`X-Xet-Signed-Range` style) so range/resume does not require a full-object capability.
alternatives: Shorter TTL only (narrows the window, keeps the class)
Source-IP binding (breaks NAT/mesh/mobile clients)

findings.scenario: Following mesh-operations.md, the operator binds synergos-control to its Mesh IP so daemons can heartbeat. Every mesh participant (including dark nodes that reconcile has not yet revoked) can sniff the segment or ARP-spoof inside the WARP tenant and capture: the admin bearer token (all orgs, reissue node keys, revoke devices), node keys (SEC-CR-11), the Cloudflare API token passed through /v1/mesh/* request bodies, and the custody admin token if custody is enabled on the same listener. On the Curare side a `CERNERE_URL=http://cernere.internal` deployment sends every user's Cernere access token as a cleartext WebSocket subprotocol on every API call.
findings.impact_ai_game: A single captured admin or Cernere token is organisation-wide access, the breach pattern that cost Rockstar and Insomniac their unreleased content. The heartbeat exception means the control plane is plaintext precisely in the deployment the docs recommend.
findings.current_state: QUIC/TLS 1.3 (rustls, ring) is correct for peer data; all HTTP/WS control and custody surfaces are plaintext in-process with optional reverse-proxy TLS; config validators allow http except for Cloudflare api_base.
findings.proposed_redesign: Terminate TLS in-process on control, custody and relay (rustls via axum-server/tokio-rustls; certificates from Infisical or ACME), with mTLS for Curare->custody and Curare->control (client cert pinned by SPKI, same verifier pattern as the QUIC layer). Config validators: `http:`/`ws:` allowed only for loopback and only when an explicit `allow_insecure_loopback=true`/NODE_ENV=development flag is set; delete the Mesh plaintext exception from control_heartbeat (or require a WARP mTLS posture claim). Curare: validate CERNERE_URL, SYNERGOS_CONTROL_URL, SYNERGOS_STORAGE_URL, MINIO_ENDPOINT at boot (https only outside development), `postgres(..., { ssl: 'require' })`, add Strict-Transport-Security. Split listeners: admin API (loopback/mTLS), heartbeat (mesh, TLS), custody transfer (public, TLS).
alternatives: Rely on WARP/Cloudflare Tunnel encryption (does not protect LAN hops, loopback-to-proxy hops, or against rogue mesh members, and is absent in on-prem deployments)

findings.scenario: A project enables `allow_project_hooks` (or a daemon hook runs `python scripts/convert.py` from the synced tree, which any peer can overwrite). The pushed script does `os.environ["SYNERGOS_IDENTITY_PASSPHRASE"]`, `SYNERGOS_NODE_KEY`, `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY` and posts them out. The same variables are visible to the third-party cloudflared binary and to any same-uid process via /proc/<pid>/environ. With the passphrase plus the key file the attacker owns the node identity; with the node key they impersonate the node to the control plane; with AWS creds they read the cold archive.
findings.impact_ai_game: Hooks are the asset-conversion extension point (Maya/FBX converters); treating them as trusted with the daemon's full secret set is the Codecov pattern (env exfiltration via a trusted build step).
findings.current_state: Secrets referenced by env-var name in TOML (good) but materialised as plain process env; children inherit everything; no secret manager client; GDrive credentials file permissions are not checked.
findings.proposed_redesign: Introduce a `SecretSource` in synergos-net (Infisical client per RULE_TECH_STACK, OS keyring via the `keyring` crate, or a 0600 secrets file / inherited fd `SYNERGOS_SECRETS_FD`), load once at boot into `secrecy::SecretString`, then `std::env::remove_var` each secret. Every `Command::new` goes through a `spawn_child()` helper that calls `env_clear()` and re-adds an allowlist (PATH, HOME, LANG, TMPDIR, SYNERGOS_* hook vars). Pass cloudflared credentials via `--credentials-file` (0600) rather than ambient env. Check mode of gdrive credentials_file (refuse group/world readable).
alternatives: Keep env but scrub children only (leaves /proc exposure and memory-resident plaintext)

findings.scenario: A render/history node runs under systemd with no HOME: the key goes to /tmp/synergos-identity.key, created with umask permissions (world-readable on many defaults) for the window before chmod; a second local user races the create or simply reads the 32 raw bytes (no passphrase configured by default). They now hold the node's ed25519 key: sign Hellos, gossip, invite tokens and chain blocks as that node forever (no revocation, SEC-CR-09). On Windows the fallback `./Synergos/identity.key` inherits the working directory's ACL.
findings.impact_ai_game: History/CI nodes are long-lived shared machines; their identity is what peers trust for every asset version they serve. Key theft on one shared workstation is undetectable identity cloning.
findings.current_state: Opt-in AES-256-GCM + Argon2id (library defaults m=19 MiB, t=2, p=1) via env passphrase; plaintext accepted even when a passphrase is set; chmod-after-write; no zeroization of the secret buffer.
findings.proposed_redesign: Default to the OS keystore (macOS Keychain, Windows DPAPI/CNG, Linux secret-service) via the `keyring` crate; file fallback only with encryption required outside `--dev`. File format v2: `magic || version || argon2{m,t,p} || salt || nonce || ct||tag` with AAD = header bytes so parameters cannot be downgraded; write with `OpenOptions::new().create_new(true).mode(0o600)` to a temp path then rename; refuse to start if no private state dir can be resolved (no /tmp or '.' fallbacks); refuse plaintext files when a passphrase is configured and migrate them; `zeroize` the secret and derived key buffers. Windows: set a DACL restricted to the current user.
alternatives: Keep file-based keys but require passphrase always (operationally painful for headless nodes; keystore is better)

findings.scenario: An artist laptop with identity.key is stolen (CircleCI/Okta pattern). The operator wants to revoke PeerId X. There is no revocation list, no certificate validity, no control-plane feed consumed by daemons: every node keeps accepting X's Hello and serving X's FileWants. The only lever is Cloudflare device revocation via manual reconcile, which does nothing for LAN/direct QUIC or relay paths. Likewise a leaked custody receipt secret or admin token forces a simultaneous restart of all parties with no overlap window.
findings.impact_ai_game: Breach containment ('侵害の歯止め') requires killing a credential in seconds; today the mean time to revoke a node is 'rebuild the mesh'. Contractor off-boarding has no cryptographic completion.
findings.current_state: PeerId = hash(pubkey) is permanent; control registry is observational and rebindable by the node; node keys can be reissued (good) but 'connector token reissue' only re-fetches the same Cloudflare token.
findings.proposed_redesign: (1) Control plane publishes a signed, monotonically versioned revocation bundle `{seq, issued_at, revoked_peer_ids[], revoked_kids[], revoked_invites[]}` signed by a control Ed25519 key whose public key is pinned in daemon config; daemons fetch every <=60 s, fail closed (deny new sessions) when the bundle is older than a configurable window, check it at accept(), connect(), stream dispatch and JOIN. (2) Identity rotation: `synergos identity rotate` generates a new key and a `KeyRotation{old_pub, new_pub, ts, sig_old, sig_new}` record that is gossiped and registered with control; peers accept the new key for the old PeerId during a grace period, after which the PeerId maps to the new key (or make PeerId a control-assigned stable id bound to the current pubkey). (3) Every HMAC/signature carries `kid`; secrets rotate with dual-key acceptance. (4) Self-signed QUIC certs get a short validity and the verifier checks `_now` (pinning stays primary).
alternatives: SPIFFE/SPIRE-style short-lived X.509 SVIDs issued by the control plane (cleaner; requires an online CA and offline-mode story for studios without connectivity)

findings.title: One ed25519 identity key signs four unrelated structures (HLO1, gossip, chain blocks, invite JSON) with no domain-separation context or version, and the gossip canonical bytes are ambiguous
findings.area: synergos-net quic/hello.rs, gossip/message.rs, chain/file_chain.rs; synergos-core invite_token.rs

evidence.quote: out.extend_from_slice(self.peer_id.0.as_bytes()); out.push(0); ...  // no context tag

out.extend_from_slice(b"peer_status"); out.extend_from_slice(peer_id.0.as_bytes()); out.extend_from_slice(origin.0.as_bytes()); ... out.extend_from_slice(status.display_name.as_bytes());  // concatenation without length prefixes
buf.extend_from_slice(&self.hash.0); ... buf.extend_from_slice(&self.version.to_le_bytes()); buf.extend_from_slice(&self.author_public_key);
let json = serde_json::to_vec(payload).expect("payload serializable"); let sig = identity.sign(&json);

findings.scenario: Today the four preimages happen to differ at byte 0 (40 hex chars, an ASCII tag, a 32-byte hash, '{'), so no immediate cross-protocol forgery exists. But any new signed message (a JSON control message, a gossip variant without a tag, a future heartbeat signature) can collide with an existing preimage and transplant a signature. Within gossip, `ConflictAlert{file_id:"doca", nodes:[""]}` and `{file_id:"doc", nodes:["a"]}` produce identical signing bytes and MessageId, enabling dedup suppression of a legitimate message or signature transplant between semantically different messages from the same signer.
findings.impact_ai_game: Signatures are what the redesign will lean on for publisher-signed revision records, membership credentials and revocation bundles; adding more message types to an unseparated signing key multiplies the collision surface.
findings.current_state: Ad-hoc per-module signing bytes; the gossip author marks the encoding as 暫定.
findings.proposed_redesign: Single `Signed<T>` envelope in synergos-net: `sig = Ed25519(ctx || 0x00 || version:u8 || canonical(T))`, where ctx comes from a registry of constants (`synergos/hello`, `synergos/gossip`, `synergos/chain`, `synergos/invite`, `synergos/node-card`, `synergos/heartbeat`, `synergos/revocation`, `synergos/revision`) and canonical(T) is deterministic, length-prefixed msgpack (or RFC 8949 §4.2.1 CBOR). Forbid direct `identity.sign(` outside the envelope module (lint). Publish test vectors shared by all crates and by the Curare TypeScript side where it verifies Synergos signatures.
alternatives: Ed25519ctx (RFC 8032 §5.1 with context) via ed25519-dalek's `sign_prehashed`/context support (equivalent separation; less portable to JS verifiers)

findings.title: Control-plane heartbeat proves possession of a bearer node key, not of the node identity: peer_id is self-asserted, unsigned and rebindable, so the registry can never be a trust anchor for the data plane

evidence.quote: let body = serde_json::json!({ "node_id": ..., "peer_id": self.peer_id.to_string(), "mesh_ip": mesh_ip, ... }); client.post(&self.config.heartbeat_url).bearer_auth(&self.node_key).json(&body)  // no signature, nonce or counter
node.synergos_peer_id = Some(req.peer_id); node.reported_mesh_ip = mesh_ip;

findings.scenario: A node key leaks (plaintext mesh HTTP per SEC-CR-06, or env per SEC-CR-07). The attacker heartbeats `{node_id: victim, peer_id: attacker_peer}`; the registry now binds the victim's node record to the attacker's PeerId. Any allowlist the redesign derives from the registry (the obvious fix for the missing membership ACL) would admit the attacker and reject the real node. Conversely, control cannot detect that a daemon's identity file was swapped.
findings.impact_ai_game: The control plane is meant to be the 'no dark nodes' authority; without proof of key possession it cannot be the root for who may serve or receive assets.
findings.current_state: Bearer node key (244-bit, blake3-hashed at rest: fine) + unauthenticated claims; the enrollment flow never captures the node's public key.
findings.proposed_redesign: Enrollment: daemon POSTs `{node_id, pubkey, proof = Ed25519("synergos/enroll/v1" || node_id || pubkey || nonce)}` using the one-time node key; control stores pubkey and derives/validates peer_id itself. Heartbeat body signed with context `synergos/heartbeat/v1` over `{node_id, peer_id, mesh_ip, version, ts, counter}`; control verifies against the enrolled pubkey, rejects counter regressions and |skew| > 2 min, and refuses peer_id changes without a KeyRotation record (SEC-CR-09). The node key then becomes a transport bearer only (or is replaced by mTLS with the node cert).
alternatives: mTLS to control with the node identity as client cert (removes the node key entirely; needs TLS on control first, SEC-CR-06)

findings.title: Receipt/capability signing uses a bespoke canonical-JSON scheme implemented twice (Rust byte-order sort / JS UTF-16 sort, different number formatting), with no kid/alg/iat/nonce and no clock-skew tolerance
findings.area: synergos-custody/src/signature.rs, handlers.rs verify; curare-server src/submissions/contract.ts canonicalJson, storage/durable-receipt.ts

evidence.quote: pairs.sort_by(|a, b| a.0.cmp(b.0));  ...  _ => value.to_string(),
.sort(([a], [b]) => a < b ? -1 : a > b ? 1 : 0).map(([k, v]) => JSON.stringify(k) + ':' + canonicalJson(v))  ...  return JSON.stringify(value);

let expires = ...min(Utc::now() + chrono::Duration::minutes(5)); let receipt = json!({"operationId":..., "verifiedDigests":[...], "durability":"durable", "locations":[state.config.node_id], "expiresAt":...});  // no kid/alg/iat/nonce
|| new Date(receipt.expiresAt) <= now) throw new VersioningError('receipt_identity_or_expiry_mismatch', 409);

findings.scenario: (a) Availability: the custody host clock drifts 6 minutes behind Curare; every receipt's expiresAt (<= now_custody + 5 min) is already in the past for Curare, so all synergos-backed confirms fail with 409 and no version can be created until an operator notices. (b) Robustness: both implementations agree today only because receipt keys are fixed ASCII and byteLength is a safe integer; a future non-ASCII/non-BMP key, a float, or a 2^53+ integer silently diverges (Rust sorts by UTF-8 bytes, JS by UTF-16 code units; serde_json prints 1e21 where JS prints 1e+21), invalidating every signature at deploy time. (c) No `kid` makes rotation impossible; no nonce means a receipt is replayable within its window (bounded by operationId).
findings.impact_ai_game: Receipts are the evidence Curare uses before a release artifact becomes a version; silent verifier divergence or clock-skew outages stall every submission across the studio.
findings.current_state: HMAC-SHA256 over hand-rolled canonical JSON; one shared fixture test; expiry min(admission, now+5 min); Curare checks identity fields and expiry only.
findings.proposed_redesign: Sign a fixed binary encoding rather than JSON: deterministic CBOR (RFC 8949 §4.2.1) or protobuf of `{kid, alg, iat, exp, nonce, operationId, opaqueObjectId, digests[], byteLength, locations[], durability}`; Ed25519 detached signature (SEC-CR-04). Curare accepts `iat <= now + 120 s` and `exp > now - 120 s` (skew window) and records nonce per operation. If JSON must stay, use RFC 8785 (JCS) libraries on both sides and extend the cross-repo fixture set to non-ASCII keys, large integers and floats; run the fixtures in both CIs.
alternatives: Keep HMAC+JSON and just add skew tolerance (fixes (a) only)

findings.title: QUIC/TLS hygiene gaps: no ALPN on either side, pinning verifier ignores validity/intermediates/server_name and the cert self-signature, auth failures are classified by error-string substring, and `enable_0rtt`/`max_udp_payload_size` are dead knobs

evidence.quote: let client_crypto = rustls::ClientConfig::builder().dangerous().with_custom_certificate_verifier(verifier).with_no_client_auth();  // no alpn_protocols
if msg.contains("PeerPinning") || msg.contains("UnknownIssuer") { SynergosNetError::Identity(...) } else { SynergosNetError::Quic(...) }
_intermediates: &[CertificateDer<'_>], _server_name: &ServerName<'_>, _ocsp: &[u8], _now: UnixTime ... self.check_peer_binding(end_entity)?;
pub max_udp_payload_size: u16, pub enable_0rtt: bool, ... max_udp_payload_size: 1452, enable_0rtt: false,  // grep: neither is read by quic/mod.rs

findings.scenario: (1) Protocol evolution: HLO1->HLO2 or a TXFR framing change cannot be negotiated; every change is a flag day, and a misdirected QUIC client cannot distinguish a Synergos endpoint from another QUIC service on the same port (RFC 9001 §8.1 requires ALPN). (2) An operator sets `enable_0rtt = true` expecting faster reconnects; nothing changes today, but a later naive implementation would make HLO1/TXFR replayable at the TLS layer. (3) A quinn/rustls upgrade changes the error text and peer-authentication failures are silently reclassified as generic Quic errors (the test accepts either).
findings.impact_ai_game: Mixed-version meshes (artist laptops lag behind the history node) are the norm in studios; without ALPN/versioning they fail opaquely, and 0-RTT misuse would turn an efficiency knob into a replay hole on asset pushes.
findings.current_state: TLS 1.3 via quinn 0.11/rustls 0.23 with the ring provider (good); ed25519-only signature scheme (good); no ALPN, no keepalive, dead knobs.
findings.proposed_redesign: Set `alpn_protocols = vec![b"synergos/1".to_vec()]` on both configs and bump on wire changes; match typed errors (`quinn::ConnectionError::TransportError` with the crypto alert code / `rustls::Error::InvalidCertificate`) instead of substrings; delete `enable_0rtt`/`max_udp_payload_size` or implement them with explicit rules (0-RTT only for idempotent content-hash GETs after `Connection::authenticated`, never for HLO1/TXFR/custody writes); regenerate the self-signed cert per bind with <= 90-day validity and have the verifier check `_now` while keeping SPKI pinning authoritative; set `keep_alive_interval` below idle timeout.
alternatives: Carry the protocol version only inside HLO1 (works for Synergos-to-Synergos but not for port sharing or relay demux)

findings.title: Relay path is plaintext WebSocket with room_id as the only secret, no join authentication, spoofable from_peer_id, and no end-to-end encryption of relayed payloads

evidence.quote: 本実装は TCP/WS のみ。TLS を被せるのは逆プロキシ (nginx / Caddy) 想定。
listen_addr: "0.0.0.0:8080".parse().unwrap(),
ClientControl::Join { room_id, .. } => { ... if let Err(reason) = rooms.join(room_id.clone(), sender) { ... } current_room = Some(room_id); }  // peer_id ignored, no challenge
Message::Binary(bytes) => { if let Some(room) = &current_room { rooms.broadcast(room, client_id, &bytes); }
let (ws_stream, _) = tokio_tungstenite::connect_async(url).await  // ws:// accepted; webpki roots only for wss

findings.scenario: The relay is the documented fallback for artists behind CGNAT. A room_id is advertised in DHT `RouteDto::Relay{server_url, room_id}` records and visible in plaintext join frames. Anyone with the room id connects to 0.0.0.0:8080, joins, receives every relayed frame (which, unlike the direct path, is not QUIC/TLS encrypted) and injects frames with an arbitrary `from_peer_id` that the client trusts.
findings.impact_ai_game: Roughly 10 % of artist-studio pairs will be relayed (Tailscale NAT data); if that path carries asset bytes it is the weakest link by far and silently downgrades every security property of the direct path.
findings.current_state: Relay client is never constructed by the daemon (dormant), but the server and client code and DESIGN present it as the third route.
findings.proposed_redesign: Make the relay a dumb forwarder of QUIC datagrams (DERP model): clients tunnel their existing pinned+mTLS QUIC session through WSS, so confidentiality, integrity and peer identity never depend on the relay. Join requires a signed challenge by the node identity plus a membership credential (SEC-CR-03) checked against the control-plane revocation bundle; room id = HMAC(project_relay_key, sorted peer ids) exchanged in the signed node card, never advertised in DHT; client refuses `ws://`; optional in-process rustls listener; per-room rate limits and idle timeout (currently parsed but unused).
alternatives: Keep application-frame relay but wrap every payload in an AEAD channel keyed by a Noise handshake (reimplements what QUIC already provides)

findings.title: Control-plane secrets are handled as static copy-paste strings: one admin bearer for everything, admin token in browser sessionStorage with no CSP, Cloudflare API token round-tripped through the browser, node_key/connector_token returned in JSON and embedded in shell commands, custody admin routes merged on the same listener

evidence.quote: pub async fn require_admin_token(State(expected): State<AdminToken>, ...) { ... if !constant_time_eq(provided.as_bytes(), expected.0.as_bytes()) { return Err(ControlError::Unauthorized); }
const TOKEN_KEY: &str = "synergos-admin-token"; ... storage.set_item(TOKEN_KEY, token)
enroll_command: Some(format!("sudo warp-cli connector new {token} && sudo warp-cli connect")), connector_token: Some(token),
pub struct RegisterNodeResponse { pub node: NodeView, pub connector_token: Option<String>, pub node_key: String, ... }
response.headers_mut().insert(header::CONTENT_TYPE, HeaderValue::from_static(mime_for(path)));  // no CSP/HSTS/X-Frame-Options
if let Some(custody) = synergos_custody::config::Config::from_env()? { router = router.merge(synergos_custody::router(custody).await?); }

findings.scenario: Any script injection in the Dioxus admin UI (no CSP) reads the admin token from sessionStorage and the Cloudflare API token from the mesh-setup form, then calls /v1/orgs/*/node-key, /v1/reconcile{revoke_dark:true} and, if custody is co-hosted, /v1/custody/reclaim for every object. Separately, connector tokens and node keys copied from the UI into terminals end up in shell history and screenshots; the bulk connector-token endpoint hands out dozens at once.
findings.impact_ai_game: The admin token is the org-wide master key over node enrollment, device revocation and (with custody) deletion of release artifacts; its exposure surface is a browser tab.
findings.current_state: Constant-time compare, env-sourced token, Debug redaction and no-store headers are present; no identity, roles, rotation, CSP, or enrollment ceremony.
findings.proposed_redesign: Authenticate admins through Cernere (OIDC/session assertion per RULE.md §1) with org-scoped roles instead of one static token; keep a break-glass token only for bootstrap with mandatory rotation and dual-token grace. Provisioning secrets become one-time claim URLs consumed by the daemon's enrollment (`synergos enroll <claim-url>` fetches node_key/connector token once over TLS, never displayed). Add CSP (`default-src 'self'`), HSTS, X-Frame-Options, nosniff on control; split listeners (admin loopback/mTLS; heartbeat mesh TLS; custody public TLS); require step-up/JIT for revoke_dark and reclaim.
alternatives: Per-admin static tokens with scopes stored hashed in the registry (interim step before Cernere integration)

findings.title: Curare credential hygiene: user tokens in CLI env/shell history and pasted into the Web UI, Cernere token relayed as a WebSocket subprotocol header, hard-coded MinIO/Postgres credentials and published ports in docker-compose, no server-side encryption on object PUTs
findings.area: curare-server src/client/cli.ts, public/api.js, src/auth/cernere-actor.ts, docker-compose.yaml, src/storage/minio-client.ts

evidence.quote: const server=process.env.CURARE_SERVER_URL; const token=process.env.CURARE_TOKEN;
const socket = new WebSocket(url, ['bearer', token]);
POSTGRES_PASSWORD: curare ... MINIO_ROOT_USER: curare  MINIO_ROOT_PASSWORD: curare-secret  (ports 5432/6379/9000/9001 published)
const command = new PutObjectCommand({ Bucket: bucket, Key: objectKey, ContentType: contentType, ChecksumSHA256: ..., IfNoneMatch: '*' });  // no ServerSideEncryption

findings.scenario: A render-farm job exports CURARE_TOKEN in a CI step; the token appears in job logs or an attacker reads it from the environment of a compromised step (Codecov pattern) and gets the human user's full Cernere identity for the token lifetime. On the Web side, a user pastes a raw 60-minute Cernere JWT into a form, so users keep long-lived tokens in text files. The bearer token in `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` is logged by intermediaries that log upgrade headers. A developer runs the shipped compose on an office LAN: MinIO root creds `curare/curare-secret` on 0.0.0.0:9000 expose every asset.
findings.impact_ai_game: Pipelines and farms are the AI/game automation path; without machine identities and keychain storage, every automation reuses a human token (cu-auth-access W24).
findings.current_state: Tokens are never persisted by the clients (good); `.env.example` is sanitized; compose is not (2026-05-13 finding CR-V-01 still open).
findings.proposed_redesign: CLI: device-code/OAuth login against Cernere, refresh handling, tokens stored in the OS keychain (`keytar`/`@napi-rs/keyring`), `CURARE_TOKEN` env accepted only with `--token-from-env` and a warning; service principals (Cernere Tool Client with scopes) for farms/CI. Server: send the Cernere token in an `Authorization` header on the WebSocket upgrade (Node `ws`/undici support headers) or exchange it for a one-time ticket, and enforce wss outside development (SEC-CR-06). Compose: credentials from env, no host port publishing by default, pinned image tags. Storage: `ServerSideEncryption: 'aws:kms'` with a per-org KMS key (or SSE-C with Curare-held per-org keys) so bucket credential theft is not plaintext asset theft; crypto-shred by key destruction on off-boarding.
alternatives: Short-lived tokens only (mitigates lifetime, not storage/logging)
sources: maps/cu-auth-access.md W5, W23, W24; maps/cu-workflow-infra.md W4

findings.title: Secret-bearing values reach logs: the IPC server debug-logs full commands including invite tokens and 1 MiB payloads, and capability signatures ride in URL query strings that proxies record

evidence.quote: tracing::debug!("Received command: {:?}", command);  // IpcCommand::ProjectJoin { invite_token, .. } and PeerSendStream { payload, .. } derive Debug
.append_pair("expires", ...).append_pair("signature", &signature).append_pair("name", name);

findings.scenario: During an incident an operator runs the daemon with RUST_LOG=debug and ships logs to a central aggregator; every `project join` token (unexpiring, SEC-CR-03) is now in the SIEM with broad read access. A CDN or nginx in front of custody keeps default access logs; each line contains a live GET/PUT capability for up to 15 minutes.
findings.impact_ai_game: Log pipelines are routinely shared with support/vendors; they become a second distribution channel for access credentials.
findings.current_state: Invite token creation deliberately avoids logging the token (project.rs:877-882); PeerId::short() and redact_path exist; but the generic Debug dump bypasses them. Curare's access log is path-only (good).
findings.proposed_redesign: Introduce `Secret<T>` newtypes (or the `secrecy` crate) with a redacting Debug for `invite_token`, `payload`, passphrases, node keys and capability signatures across synergos-ipc, control and custody; log only the command discriminant plus non-secret fields; add a tracing layer that drops fields named token/secret/signature; move the capability signature out of the query string (SEC-CR-05); document log retention and access.
alternatives: Only lower the log level (does not survive the next debug session)
sources: AIFormat/common/REVIEW_VULNERABILITY.md §1 (機密情報の露出: ログ・エラーメッセージ)

findings.title: Tauri GUI ships with CSP disabled, no updater plugin or signature verification, and no code-signing/notarization configuration

evidence.quote: "security": { "csp": null }
tauri = { version = "2", features = [] }  tauri-plugin-opener = "2"  tauri-plugin-dialog = "2"  // no tauri-plugin-updater
"bundle": { "active": true, "targets": "all", "icon": [...] }  // no macOS.signingIdentity / windows.certificateThumbprint / createUpdaterArtifacts

findings.scenario: Artists install an unsigned bundle (Gatekeeper/SmartScreen warnings train them to click through), and because there is no update channel the vulnerable build stays on laptops for months, the exact device class that was the entry point in the Rockstar/Okta/LastPass incidents. With CSP null, any HTML injection in the React UI (e.g. a peer-supplied display_name or file name rendered via dangerouslySetInnerHTML in a future component) gains access to every Tauri command, i.e. full daemon IPC and config writes.
findings.impact_ai_game: The GUI is the artist-facing surface and the most numerous installed component; it needs the strongest distribution integrity, not the weakest.
findings.current_state: Minimal capability set (core/opener/dialog) is good; everything in local-app REVIEW_VULNERABILITY_LOCAL.md §4 (署名・ハッシュ検証, HTTPS 配信, ダウングレード対策) is absent.
findings.proposed_redesign: Add `tauri-plugin-updater` with the minisign public key embedded in tauri.conf.json, HTTPS update manifest served from the control plane or a signed static bucket, version monotonicity (reject downgrades) and rollback-safe install; sign and notarize bundles in CI (Apple Developer ID + notarization, Windows Authenticode via HSM/Azure Trusted Signing) with SLSA provenance; set a strict CSP (`default-src 'self'; connect-src ipc: http://ipc.localhost; img-src 'self' data:`); add `dangerousDisableAssetCspModification: false` (default) and keep capabilities minimal.
alternatives: Distribute through platform stores (Mac App Store / winget) which enforce signing but constrain the IPC model

findings.title: No encryption at rest anywhere in the asset path: custody objects, history-node objects, S3/GDrive cold storage (keyed by raw content hash) and MinIO objects are plaintext with no per-project keys, so credential theft equals asset theft and off-boarding cannot crypto-shred

evidence.quote: let mut file = tokio::fs::OpenOptions::new().create_new(true).write(true).open(&partial.0).await?; ... file.write_all(&chunk).await?; hash.update(&chunk); ... durable_file::publish(&partial.0, &self.path(key, "data")).await?;  // raw bytes to disk
pub fn object_key(project_id: &str, hash: &str) -> String { format!("{}/{hash}", blake3::hash(project_id.as_bytes()).to_hex()) }
let bytes = tokio::fs::read(path).await?; store.put(&self.object_path(key), PutPayload::from_bytes(Bytes::from(bytes)))
new PutObjectCommand({ Bucket: bucket, Key: objectKey, ContentType: contentType, ChecksumSHA256: ..., IfNoneMatch: '*' })  // no SSE

findings.scenario: A single leaked S3/MinIO credential, a stolen history-node disk, or a custody volume snapshot exposes every version of every asset in plaintext (LastPass/Insomniac pattern). Cold-storage keys equal the content hash, so an attacker with a known asset can confirm its presence without reading it. When a contractor's project ends, or an AI-Act/GDPR deletion is required, there is no key to destroy; history nodes keep every version by design, so deletion means rewriting history on every node.
findings.impact_ai_game: Studios must show per-tenant key isolation and crypto-shred on off-boarding to pass TPN/ISO-style assessments (research §7); AI datasets with personal data need provable deletion (AI Act Art. 10(5)) that a plaintext every-version store cannot give.
findings.current_state: Integrity is strong (BLAKE3/SHA-256 verified end to end); confidentiality at rest is entirely delegated to the OS/bucket.
findings.proposed_redesign: Envelope encryption: per-project KEK held in Infisical/KMS (encryption context {org, project}); per-blob DEK (AES-256-GCM or XChaCha20-Poly1305) wrapped by the KEK and stored in the manifest/history index and custody admission; AAD = {org, project, plaintext_blake3}. Custody keeps hashing the plaintext stream for verification, then encrypts on the way to disk (receipt still attests the plaintext digest). Cold-storage object keys become HMAC(project_key, hash). MinIO: SSE-KMS per org bucket prefix. Off-boarding/legal deletion = destroy the KEK after the retention lock lapses while manifests keep hashes for auditability.
alternatives: Full-disk/bucket-level encryption only (no tenant separation, no crypto-shred, keys shared with the host)
sources: AIFormat/web/REVIEW_VULNERABILITY_WEB.md §3 (保存データの暗号化 at-rest)

coverage_notes: Read all 11 available maps and all 4 research notes in full (tails of the research notes are source lists). The 12th map, maps/sy-clients-docs.md, was absent at start, after the other 11 maps, and on a final retry before code work; this audit therefore did not benefit from its coverage of the Tauri GUI/CLI/docs beyond what I verified directly in synergos-tauri (tauri.conf.json, Cargo.toml, capabilities, lib.rs/ipc.rs headers). Every finding above was verified at file:line in Synergos or Curare (nothing was taken from the maps unverified except where the evidence entry explicitly says 'per <map>', used only for secondary lines in SEC-CR-05 and SEC-CR-14 whose primary lines I verified). Items checked and found acceptable (no finding): CSPRNG usage (OsRng for keys/salts/nonces, uuid v4 via getrandom for tokens/node keys, rand::thread_rng for STUN tx ids); TLS versions (QUIC = TLS 1.3 via quinn 0.11.11/rustls 0.23.44 ring; reqwest rustls-tls for HTTPS clients; rustls 0.21.12 only transitively present); timing-safe comparisons (custody Mac::verify_slice, control constant_time_eq, Curare timingSafeEqual); Argon2id library defaults (argon2 0.5.3: m=19 MiB, t=2, p=1 meets OWASP minimum, though parameters are not recorded in the file header, see SEC-CR-08); ed25519-only TLS signature scheme restriction; cargo audit present in Synergos CI. Deliberately left to other lenses: project membership ACL at accept()/dispatch, DHT record authentication, per-peer resource limits/DoS, IPC authorization model, hook sandboxing, Curare authz model, supply-chain pinning beyond the crypto scope. Severity for SEC-CR-14 assumes the relay is deployed as documented; it is dormant in the current daemon.
